Members of the __`r com_full`__ (__`r com_acr`__) are interested in understanding the changes in wildlife condition and behaviour that they are noticing on the land. The health and abundance of wildlife populations is relied upon by members of `r com_acr` to support a traditional way of life. To ensure the sustainability of this way of life it is important to understand both how many animals, such as moose, are available for harvest every year and what the drivers of change are in the abundance of wildlife over time. These concerns led to the initiation of this wildlife monitoring program in 2023.
<br>
<br>
In 2023, `r com_acr` created a Community Knowledge Committee comprising both elders and youths to lead this project. This Community Knowledge Committee shares knowledge and disseminates information about the program across age ranges and the region. The Committee engages with ABMI staff about program updates, monitoring methods, study design, site locations, analysis, and integration of Indigenous knowledge indicators.

<br>

<br>

The Committee deployed 18 cameras between late September 2023 and October 2024. These cameras were primarily deployed along the Old Conklin Road near Lac La Biche (see Figure below) in clusters of 4 cameras. Cameras were deployed based on the knowledge of the land, areas of interest by the committee, and areas of oil sands disturbance.
<br>
<br>
The goal of the program is to evaluate the specific oil sands disturbance type of **pipelines** and **roads** compared to reference (low disturbance) areas. To achieve this, 2 clusters of 4 cameras were deployed along pipeline right of ways and roads at distances up to 100 metres. Additionally, 2 clusters of cameras were deployed in reference areas picked by the community.

## Camera Refresh and Image Processing

The wildlife cameras were refreshed (given new SD cards and batteries) in the field by the Community Knowledge Committee in 2024 and 2025. The CKC members uploaded and tagged all of the camera images on the online platform [WildTrax](www.wildtrax.ca)[^1]. WildTrax is an online platform developed by the [Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute](www.abmi.ca) for users of environmental sensors such as remote cameras to provide support with processing, standardizing, and sharing data. Initial results from this first year of data collected at the 18 cameras are presented here in this report. 

[^1]: `r com_acr` images and wildlife tags can be viewed using [this link](https://portal.wildtrax.ca/home/camera-deployments.html?sensorId=CAM&projectId=2929) to the WildTrax platform. Note that viewers will need to have a WildTrax account with the appropriate permissions from the community and be logged in to see the images.

# Independent Detections Over Time

With camera data, one useful metric to track over time is the number of "independent" detections captured for each species. In this case, an independent detection is defined as an image or collection of images captured for a given species that can be thought of as a single detection event.

In the figure below we present the number of independent detections for each of the 8 focal species detected in the `r com_acr` project. We use a 30 minute time interval to separate detection events; that is, images captured within 30 minutes of each other count toward a single detection and images with a gap of greater than 30 minutes between them count as multiple independent detections. Images that are captured of the same species over less than 30 minutes are assumed to be of the same individual, or group of individuals.

```{r}

```

The y-axis represents the number of detections captured, which is pooled across all the cameras from the project. Note that the y-axis of the plots for each species may differ depending on the number of detections captured.

```{r}
  html <- glue::glue(
    '<div style="text-align: center;">
       <img src="{rel_path}" style="width:80%;">
       <figcaption style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 0.5em;">
         <strong>Figure 3{letter}.</strong> Independent detections of <strong>{title}</strong> across the study time period.
       </figcaption>
     </div>\n\n'
  )
  
  cat(html)
}

cat(":::\n")

```

+ **White-tailed deer** were primarily detected in the summer months of June, July, and August. 
+ Because they are nocturnal, detection of **Black Bears** began in May, and peaked in late June and early July.
+ **Moose** were consistently detected year round, as were **Coyote** and **Canada Lynx**.
+ Detections of **Snowshoe Hare** were also consistent year round, with the exception of the later summer months (August).
+ **Woodland Caribou** and **Gray Wolf** detections were infrequent and sporadic across the duration of the project.

# Temporal Activity Patterns

Given that camera traps operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and can record animal motion down to second-level precision, they represent a powerful tool to explore and contrast the activity patterns of the species they detect. Such analyses can give insight into competition, predation, and coexistence.

In this section we present the temporal (diel) activity patterns for each of the 8 focal species from the `r com_acr` cameras. The x-axis of each of the following plots represents the 24-hr daily cycle, and the line represents the relative activity level detected by the cameras. This data is pooled across all 18 cameras in the project.

```{r}
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: asis

# Set folder containing the plots
file_names <- paste0("Activity ", species, ".png")
figure_letters <- letters[1:length(species)]

cat("::: panel-tabset\n\n")

for (i in seq_along(species)) {
  title <- species[i]
  letter <- figure_letters[i]
  img_path <- here::here("Figures/OMGD19", file_names[i])
  rel_path <- fs::path_rel(img_path, start = getwd())
  
  cat("### ", title, " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
  
  # Render the image and caption
  html <- glue::glue(
    '<div style="text-align: center;">
       <img src="{rel_path}" style="width:80%;">
       <figcaption style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 0.5em;">
         <strong>Figure 4{letter}.</strong> Daily activity pattern of <strong>{title}</strong> based on camera trap detections.
       </figcaption>
     </div>\n\n'
  )
  
  cat(html)
}

cat(":::\n")


```

+ **White-tailed deer** are primarily active during twilight hours, specifically at dawn and dusk. This pattern is known as *crepuscular*. The majority of the activity, however, was captured during the dawn hours (6:00 to 9:00). 
+ **Black Bear** were similarily crepuscular, although the peak was much more pronounced during the dusk hours (between 18:00 and 24:00).
+ Based on the cameras in the `r com_acr` project, **Moose** were primarily active during the night time (00:00 to 6:00).
+ **Coyote** and **Snowshoe Hare** were similar to Moose, but had slightly elevated (and increasing) activity levels throughout the evening hours.
+ **Canada Lynx** activity peaked during the midday (12:00). **Caribou** were similar, with a slightly earlier, and more pronounced, peak (10:00).
+ Finally, **Gray Wolf** showed a slightly crepuscular tendency, however the dusk activity peak was more extreme. 

# Species Co-Occurences

Camera trap data are being increasingly used to model multiple species communities, and we can use this data to explore the co-occurrence patterns of the species in the community.

Figure 5 below displays pairwise correlations between the species on the left and the species on the top row. Blue colours indicate positive correlation, meaning that the two species are positively associated with one another. Red colours indicate the opposite, that where you have high counts of one species you likely have low counts of the other (and vice versa).

# Species Density

In addition to the number of images and counts of independent detections, we can estimate the density of each species at each camera. Density is the number of animals per unit area, which translates to abundance when scaled up to a larger region of interest. 

To estimate the density of each wildlife species at each camera, we used the Time in Front of Camera (TIFC) approach (@becker2022applying). This method has previously been used to estimate densities of unmarked populations of both white-tailed deer and moose in the boreal region of Alberta. Similar to quadrat sampling, the TIFC approach involves (for each camera) multiplying the number of animals observed by the total time they spend in front of the camera, which is then divided by the product of the area sampled by the camera and the total time the camera was operating. This calculation yields an estimate of animals per unit area (i.e., 'density').

The following map displays the spatial distribution in densities of the 8 focal species between the 18 cameras of the OMGD19 camera project. Note that cameras with no detections of a particular species (i.e., a density of '0') are represented with a black circle.

<br>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" style="background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 5px;"}
You can hover over each camera location to see the calculated density of each species at that deployment.
:::

```{r}
#| label: map-species-density
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

densities_to_map <- locations_for_map |>
  left_join(df_density_sum) |>
  select(-project) |>
  mutate(density_km2 = ifelse(density_km2 > 5, 5, density_km2)) |>
  mutate(log_density = log10(density_km2 + 1))

# Species palette as a list
species_palette <- list(
  "White-tailed Deer"  = "#3A86FF",  
  "Snowshoe Hare"      = "#E63946",  
  "Moose"              = "#06D6A0",  
  "Canada Lynx"        = "#FFBE0B",  
  "Black Bear"         = "#8338EC",  
  "Woodland Caribou"   = "#FB5607",  
  "Coyote"             = "#3366CC",  
  "Gray Wolf"          = "#FF006E"
)

buffer <- 0.1

# Create base map
leaf_map <- leaflet(width = "90%", height = "750px") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", group = "Gray Canvas") |>
  fitBounds(
    lng1 = min(densities_to_map$longitude) - buffer,
    lat1 = min(densities_to_map$latitude) - buffer,
    lng2 = max(densities_to_map$longitude) + buffer,
    lat2 = max(densities_to_map$latitude) + buffer
  ) |>
  addFullscreenControl() |>
  addResetMapButton()

max_log <- max(densities_to_map$log_density, na.rm = TRUE)

# Loop over species and add circle markers for each base group
for (sp in species) {
  
  data <- densities_to_map |> 
  filter(species_common_name == sp) |>
  mutate(
    scaled_radius = pmax(log_density / max_log * 15, 4),
    fill_color = ifelse(density_km2 == 0, "#222222", species_palette[[sp]]),
    label_text = ifelse(
      density_km2 == 0,
      paste0(
        "<table>",
        "<tr><td>Camera location:</td><td align='right'><b>", location, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td>Treatment:</td><td align='right'><b>", treatment, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td colspan='2'><i>No detections at this location</i></td></tr>",
        "</table>"
      ),
      paste0(
        "<table>",
        "<tr><td>Camera location:</td><td align='right'><b>", location, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td>Treatment:</td><td align='right'><b>", treatment, "</b></td></tr>",
        "<tr><td>", species_common_name, " Density:</td><td align='right'><b>",
        round(density_km2, 2), " per km²</b></td></tr>",
        "</table>"
      )
    )
  )
  
  leaf_map <- leaf_map |>
    addCircleMarkers(
      data = data,
      lng = ~longitude,
      lat = ~latitude,
      radius = ~scaled_radius,
      fillColor = ~fill_color,
      fillOpacity = 0.85,
      stroke = TRUE,
      color = "#FFFFFF",
      weight = 1,
      group = sp,
      label = ~ lapply(label_text, HTML),
      labelOptions = labelOptions(
        html = TRUE,
        direction = "top",
        textsize = "14px",
        style = list(
          "padding" = "6px"
        )
      )
    )
}

leaf_map <- leaf_map |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = species,
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE),
    position = "topleft"
  )

tags$div(
  style = "display: flex; justify-content: center;",
  leaf_map)

```

# Evaluating Oil Sands Disturbances

In this section we present the results from `r com_acr` camera deployments evaluating the impact of specific oil sands stressors on wildlife within `r com_acr`: **pipelines** and **roads**. The effect of these stressors on species' density is evaluated by comparing values to a **reference** (low disturbance) area. 

The following plots show the density of each species at each cluster of cameras. Each point represents the average density value among the cameras of the cluster. For instance, the 4 cameras that belong to the 'MNA 19-6' cluster (which is a reference cluster) had white-tailed deer density values of 4.75, 4.79, 5, and 3.36 animals per km<sup>2</sup>, for an average density of 4.47. This is represented by the top point in the Reference column of Figure 6a below. 

There are 3 reference clusters, 1 linear features cluster (pipelines), and 2 road features cluster. The tabs can be used to toggle through each individual species results. 

We can also compare the results from the 6 camera clusters deployed by `r com_acr` to those deployed as part of the broader regional OSM monitoring done by the ABMI. The ABMI deploys clusters of cameras (called 'Joint Environmental Monitoring Sites', or JEMS) in a similar fashion to `r com_acr`, targeting the physical footprint and adjacent areas of oil sands industry disturbances (@Bayne2021OSMFramework). There are two stressors examined by both the `r com_acr` cameras and the regional monitoring done by the ABMI: **linear features** and **roads**, as well as **reference (low disturbance)** areas. In the figures below for each species, we also plot out the values obtained from ABMI JEM sites alongside the `r com_acr` values.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" style="background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 5px;"}
Click on each **Data Source** (e.g., 'OSM Regional Monitoring') within each of the plot legends to hide or display the data associated with each source.
Hover over each point to view which cluster the value is associated with.
:::

```{r}
#| label: set-up
#| echo: false
#| include: true
#| eval: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

data <- df_density_os |>
  mutate(project = factor(
    project, levels = c("OSM Regional Monitoring", "OMGD19 Local Monitoring"))) |>
  group_by(species_common_name) |>
  mutate(rank = if_else(
    project == "OSM Regional Monitoring",
    dense_rank(desc(density_km2)),
    NA_integer_  # Don't rank OMGD19 — set to NA
  )) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(is.na(rank) | rank > 3)
  
figure_letters <- letters[1:length(species)]

plot_list <- list()

for (sp in seq_along(species)) {
  
  title <- species[sp]
  letter <- figure_letters[sp]
  
  d <- data[data$species_common_name == title, ]
  
  p <- d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = density_km2, color = project,
             text = paste0(
               "Cluster: ", site,
               "<br>",
               "Density: ", round(density_km2, 2)
             ))) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("OMGD19 Local Monitoring" = species_colours[[title]], 
               "OSM Regional Monitoring" = "grey70"),
    name = "Data Source: "
  ) +
  labs(x = "") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 13),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14))
  
  plot_list[[title]] <- p
  
}

```

:::

+ **White-tailed deer** have the highest densities across both stressor treatments and the reference areas among all the species. Density was highest in the reference clusters, and lower in both the linear features cluster and the two roads clusters.
+ The opposite pattern was found for **Black Bear**, where lower densities were found in the reference clusters and higher densities in the stressor treatments, particularly the two road clusters.
+ **Moose** densities were relatively low across all camera clusters, especially in areas of linear features (pipelines).
+ **Coyotes** were attracted to to road features, but not linear features. The same pattern was observed for **Snowshoe Hare** and **Canada Lynx**. 
+ **Caribou** and **Wolf** densities (and overall detections) were very low across all clusters, making it difficult to assess patterns and response to stressors. However, wolf density does seem to be higher in reference areas. 

# Species Predictions

The ABMI compiles all remote camera data collected in Alberta’s boreal region (including the Oil Sands Region) and uses it to develop habitat models for each species. These models incorporate species’ responses to land cover (e.g., vegetation and forest types), human disturbance, and climate variables.

The maps below show one output from these models: the predicted probability of species presence within the OMGD19 area of interest. The area is divided into 1 km<sup>2</sup> pixels, and for each pixel, the model estimates the probability of presence for each species based on the habitat and disturbance present in that location.

<br>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" style="background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 5px;"}
Use the buttons on the top right of the map to toggle through each species' predictions. You can also turn on Satellite Imagery and use the NONE (Blank) button to view the imagery underneath the predictions.
:::

```{r}
#| label: map-species-predictions
#| include: true
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Load AOI
aoi <- st_read(paste0(g_drive_cbme, "OMGD19/AOI/OMG19 Area of Interest.shp"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Load rasters for each species
raster_list <- species |>
  set_names() |>
  map(~ terra::rast(paste0(g_drive_cbme, "OMGD19/Predictions/", .x, " OMGD19.tif")))

raster_list_clamped <- map(raster_list, ~ terra::clamp(.x, lower = 0, upper = 0.60, values = TRUE))

domain_raw <- c(0, 0.601)

pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "skyblue", "gold", "red"))(100),
  domain = domain_raw,
  na.color = "transparent"
)

# Start building the leaflet map
map <- leaflet(width = "90%", height = "750px") |>
  addMapPane(name = "Basemap", zIndex = 410) |>
  addMapPane(name = "Satellite Imagery", zIndex = 420) |>
  addMapPane(name = "Species Rasters", zIndex = 430) |>
  addMapPane(name = "AOI Boundary", zIndex = 440) |>
  #addMapPane(name = "Camera Locations", zIndex = 450) |>
  addTiles(group = "Basemap", options = tileOptions(opacity = 1, pane = "Basemap")) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite Imagery", options = leafletOptions(pane = "Satellite Imagery")) |>
  addFullscreenControl() |>
  addResetMapButton() |>
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomright", options = scaleBarOptions(imperial = FALSE)) |>
  addMiniMap(position = "bottomright") |>
  addPolylines(data = aoi, color = "#0a0909", weight = 2, smoothFactor = 0.2, opacity = 1.0, fill = FALSE, options = leafletOptions(pane = "AOI Boundary"))

for (sp in species) {
  map <- map |>
    addRasterImage(
      raster_list_clamped[[sp]],
      colors = pal,
      opacity = 0.8,
      group = sp,
      options = leafletOptions(pane = "Species Rasters")
    )
}

map <- map |>
  addTiles(group = "NONE (Blank)", options = tileOptions(opacity = 0)) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = domain_raw,
    opacity = 1,
    title = "Probability of<br>Species Presence:",
    position = "bottomright",
    labFormat = labelFormat(
      transform = function(x) x * 100,
      digits = 0,
      suffix = "%"
    )
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c("Satellite Imagery"),
    baseGroups = c(species, "NONE (Blank)"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  ) |>
  hideGroup("Satellite Imagery")

# Print map

htmltools::tags$div(
  style = "display: flex; justify-content: center;",
  map)

```
